q: What is the first-line emergency treatment for acute anaphylaxis, and what serum marker confirms the diagnosis retroactively?
a: Intramuscular (IM) epinephrine (1:1,000 dilution, 0.3–0.5 mg in adults) injected into the anterolateral thigh. Serum tryptase (elevated within 1–2 hours of symptom onset) confirms mast cell degranulation.

q: A patient presenting with recurrent episodes of non-pruritic, non-pitting angioedema without urticaria and recurrent abdominal pain has low C4. What is the underlying pathophysiology and diagnostic confirmation?
a: Hereditary Angioedema caused by C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency or dysfunction, leading to unchecked kallikrein activity and excessive bradykinin accumulation. Confirmed by low C4 levels and decreased functional C1 inhibitor activity.

q: How do you differentiate Acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency from Hereditary Angioedema in an older adult presenting with angioedema?
a: Acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency is associated with underlying lymphoproliferative disorders (e.g., NHL) or autoimmunity and presents with low C1q levels, whereas Hereditary Angioedema has normal C1q levels.

q: An individual with an asymptomatic immunodeficiency experiences severe hypotension, bronchospasm, and hives during a packed red blood cell transfusion. What is the diagnosis and prevention strategy?
a: Selective IgA deficiency with pre-existing anti-IgA antibodies reacting to donor IgA. Prevent future reactions by administering washed red blood cells or products from IgA-deficient donors.

q: A 25-year-old patient with recurrent sinus infections and bronchiectasis has normal total B cell counts but severely low serum IgG, IgA, and IgM. What is the diagnosis and primary long-term management?
a: Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID), characterized by defective B-cell differentiation into plasma cells. Managed with lifelong Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG) replacement.

q: A 9-month-old male infant presents with recurrent Streptococcus pneumoniae otitis media and pneumonia. Physical exam reveals absent tonsils. Lab work shows markedly decreased CD19+/CD20+ B cells and low immunoglobulins. What is the genetic defect?
a: Mutation in the Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) gene on the X chromosome (X-linked Agammaglobulinemia), leading to failure of pre-B cell maturation.

q: A 3-month-old infant with chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive, persistent oral candidiasis, and an absent thymic shadow on chest X-ray is diagnosed with Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID). What are the two most common genetic causes?
a: X-linked recessive IL-2Rγ chain subunit defect (most common) and autosomal recessive Adenosine Deaminase (ADA) deficiency, leading to toxic accumulation of dATP in lymphocytes.

q: A child presents with severe eczema, retained primary teeth, high serum IgE, eosinophilia, and recurrent 'cold' (non-inflammatory) staphylococcal abscesses. What is the mutated gene and altered immunologic helper cell pathway?
a: Mutation in STAT3 (Hyper-IgE Syndrome / Job Syndrome), leading to impaired Th17 differentiation and deficient IL-17 production, disrupting neutrophil recruitment.

q: What classic clinical triad characterizes Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome, and what cellular mechanism is defective?
a: Triad of eczema, thrombocytopenia (with microthrombocytes/small platelets), and recurrent sinopulmonary infections. Caused by WAS gene mutations disrupting actin cytoskeleton reorganization in leukocytes and platelets.

q: A patient with recurrent granulomatous abscesses caused by Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus is suspected of having Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD). What is the enzyme defect and diagnostic test of choice?
a: Defect in NADPH oxidase (impaired production of reactive oxygen species like H2O2 and O2•–). Confirmed by abnormal dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry (decreased fluorescence) or negative nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) test.

q: An infant presents with delayed umbilical cord separation (>30 days after birth), marked leukocytosis (neutrophils > 50,000/μL), and skin infections devoid of pus formation. What is the underlying surface receptor deficiency?
a: Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency type 1 (LAD-1), caused by an autosomal recessive defect in the CD18 integrin (β2 integrin / LFA-1), preventing leukocyte adhesion and extravasation.

q: A patient with recurrent Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia has elevated serum IgM but absent serum IgG, IgA, and IgE. What cell surface ligand interaction is defective?
a: Defect in CD40 Ligand (CD40L / CD154) expressed on activated CD4+ T cells (Hyper-IgM Syndrome), which prevents interaction with CD40 on B cells, blocking class-switch recombination.

q: Ten days after starting penicillin, a patient develops fever, urticarial rash, joint pain, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Lab tests show low serum C3 and C4 levels. What hypersensitivity type is responsible?
a: Type III hypersensitivity (Serum Sickness), mediated by systemic immune complex (IgG-antigen) deposition that activates the classical complement cascade, lowering serum C3/C4.

q: A patient on allopurinol develops fever, diffuse morbilliform eruption, facial swelling, peripheral eosinophilia (>1,500/μL), and elevated serum transaminases 4 weeks after drug initiation. What is the diagnosis?
a: DRESS Syndrome (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms), a severe T-cell mediated drug reaction with multi-organ involvement (most commonly liver and kidney).

q: What is the most effective single pharmacotherapy for long-term control of moderate-to-severe Allergic Rhinitis?
a: Intranasal corticosteroid spray (e.g., fluticasone, mometasone), which inhibits local inflammatory cytokine release and inflammatory cell influx.

q: A patient with birch pollen allergy experiences localized itching and tingling of the lips and soft palate after eating raw apples and peaches. What is the mechanism of this condition?
a: Oral Allergy Syndrome (Pollen-Food Allergy Syndrome), caused by IgE cross-reactivity between airborne pollen proteins (e.g., Bet v 1 in birch) and homologous heat-labile proteins in raw fruits/vegetables.

q: A young adult presents with recurrent, severe Neisseria meningitidis infections. Screening tests show decreased CH50 activity. Which complement components are most likely deficient?
a: Deficient Terminal Complement Components (C5, C6, C7, C8, or C9), impairing the formation of the Membrane Attack Complex (MAC / C5b-9).

q: A newborn with tetralogy of Fallot develops tetany. Labs show serum Ca2+ 6.2 mg/dL and elevated serum phosphate. What is the microdeletion and embryological structure failed in development?
a: 22q11.2 microdeletion (DiGeorge Syndrome), due to failure of third and fourth pharyngeal pouches to develop, resulting in thymic and parathyroid hypoplasia.

q: A runner experiences generalized pruritus, hives, and wheezing specifically when jogging within 2 hours after eating a meal containing wheat. What is the diagnosis and acute management strategy?
a: Food-Dependent Exercise-Induced Anaphylaxis (FDEIA). Managed acutely with IM epinephrine, and prevented by refraining from exercise for 4 hours after consuming trigger foods (e.g., gliadin/wheat).

q: A 42-year-old patient with severe asthma and chronic rhinosinusitis presents with peripheral neuropathy (mononeuritis multiplex), skin nodules, and eosinophilia > 15%. Serology is positive for MPO-ANCA (p-ANCA). What vasculitis is this?
a: Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA / Churg-Strauss syndrome), a small-to-medium vessel necrotizing vasculitis. Eosinophilic myocarditis is the primary cause of mortality.
